body: What does this have to do with HTML?

Traditional fragment navigation is [defined by HTML](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#scroll-to-fragid). Scroll to text is an extension of this behavior; as such, much of the draft spec is monkey patching HTML (with a few additions to DOM and CSSOM-View).

I think the new additions (i.e. non-monkeypatching; e.g. how to parse and process the directive text) probably fits best in HTML but I'm happy to take maintainer advice on where to place things.

This sounds great to me; thanks for working on this!

One thing to be aware of is that nearby portions of the spec are undergoing a rewrite in #6315. However, I don't think it should significantly effect your work, and those of us working on the rewrite will take care of any merge conflicts that come up. Maybe give that a brief skim, to confirm my instincts there.

> Traditional fragment navigation is [defined by HTML](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#scroll-to-fragid). Scroll to text is an extension of this behavior; as such, much of the draft spec is monkey patching HTML (with a few additions to DOM and CSSOM-View).

I guess that makes sense. It just seems strange to me that something that changes nothing about HTML would be part of the HTML spec.

It changes how navigation works, including navigation of HTML documents, which is all defined by the HTML Standard. In theory we only get to define how fragments work for `text/html`, but in practice we also define it for all MIME types that end up rendering as a document at least. Also, as it happens, most things are in scope for the HTML Standard: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#abstract.

(I'm going to mark your comments and this one as resolved. If you'd like to discuss this further please reach out via https://whatwg.org/chat.)

I'm sorry for the silence - I got pulled away on other things and didn't have a chance to complete this. However, I've carved out some time now and am making a push until I can finish this.

I have a few process questions: 

- I'm currently fixing the outstanding issues in the WICG repo first before starting a merge into HTML. Does this seem like a reasonable approach?
- For parts of the WICG spec that seem settled or utility, should I break them off and merge to HTML early? Or do the editors prefer a single mega-PR that includes the whole feature?
- @annevk, you've reviewed a number of my changes already so I've typically been tagging you (thanks!). Is this ok? Is there a process for reviewer selection? Should I involve other reviewers?
- On a related note: should I be requesting reviews for each of the fixes and changes in the WICG spec? Or would it be better to request a fuller review once the issues in the WICG are resolved or mostly-resolved? Or just wait for review when I put up a PR into HTML?
- What's the best place to ask questions? I sometimes find bits in the HTML spec that seem like bugs (but more likely I'm misunderstanding something) - should I just file issues here or is there a mailing list/IRC that might be better suited?

Speaking for myself here, but I'd also be interested in @annevk's take...

> * I'm currently fixing the outstanding issues in the WICG repo first before starting a merge into HTML. Does this seem like a reasonable approach?

This seems reasonable to me.

> * For parts of the WICG spec that seem settled or utility, should I break them off and merge to HTML early? Or do the editors prefer a single mega-PR that includes the whole feature?

> * On a related note: should I be requesting reviews for each of the fixes and changes in the WICG spec? Or would it be better to request a fuller review once the issues in the WICG are resolved or mostly-resolved? Or just wait for review when I put up a PR into HTML?

As editor, I tend to prefer a single mega-PR as it reduces review burden and allows me to fit in the review between other work, instead of constantly revisiting the topic.

If others (especially other implementers) are more involved, then getting their review on smaller changes can be helpful.

> * What's the best place to ask questions? I sometimes find bits in the HTML spec that seem like bugs (but more likely I'm misunderstanding something) - should I just file issues here or is there a mailing list/IRC that might be better suited?

Filing issues here is good, or using https://whatwg.org/chat.

Sorry I missed this. I think I largely agree with @domenic as well. My thoughts:

1. If there's some refactoring needed that can be done standalone, I'd prefer that.
2. If the specification that's being integrated needs more changes it's probably best to make them there first. Ideally once we land the feature in HTML it won't need any further tweaks. (New features on top is a separate matter, of course.)
FYI, we [plan to ship text fragments](https://groups.google.com/a/mozilla.org/g/dev-platform/c/1F1vsI0Q1dI/m/LrCGgCuFDgAJ) in Firefox 131.

I realized we should probably modify https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-id-attribute to have a conformance requirement prohibiting `id=""` values which look like `:~:text=`. Maybe any that start with `:~:` in general.
Probably values that _contain_ `:~:` then, to avoid collision with e.g. https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#the-id-attribute:~:text=no%20other%20restrictions .

> Probably values that _contain_ `:~:` then

This, because [text directives](https://wicg.github.io/scroll-to-text-fragment/#text-directives) are just one of possibly future other [fragment directives](https://wicg.github.io/scroll-to-text-fragment/#the-fragment-directive) (there could be `:~:image` for example).

I uploaded an HTML file containing Schema.org structured data, but it’s not being interpreted correctly. Here’s what’s happening:

JSON-LD markup appears as raw text instead of being parsed.

When testing via Google’s Rich Results Test, it shows errors related to improperly formatted schema.

The <script type="application/ld+json"> section seems to be ignored when embedded from Gist.

Tried switching to microdata format, but it still doesn’t validate properly.

I also encountered similar schema validation errors while working with structured data on [getpoliceclearanceph.com](https://getpoliceclearanceph.com/). Does anyone know if Gist has limitations on structured data support?

I tried implementing the Scroll-To-Text Fragment feature in my project hosted on GitHub Pages, but it’s not working as expected.

I added #:~:text=target-text in the URL, but it doesn't scroll to the exact text.

The feature works fine in Google Chrome, but doesn't work in Firefox or Safari.

No JavaScript errors in the console, so I’m not sure if it's a GitHub Pages limitation.

Other websites, like https://getpoliceclearanceph.com/, work fine with this feature.
Please ask questions about how to use web platform features on other sites, like Stack Overflow. This repository is for developing the HTML Standard, not for help with web development.

Dear all,

the [W3C Publishing Maintenance Working Group](https://www.w3.org/groups/wg/pm/) has started working on an Annotation feature for EPUB publications, as recently [chartered](https://www.w3.org/2025/02/pmwg-charter.html). Scroll-to-text would play an essential role in this (see, for example, the discussion in [issue 2763](https://github.com/w3c/epub-specs/issues/2763)). However, we would need a finalized version that we could also normatively refer to from our final recommendation. Hence our question: is there an expected timeline for this PR to be incorporated in HTML? Thx.
